title: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza
description: Israel has warned Hamas that it will increase strikes on Gaza following concern over launches of kites, drones and balloons from the territory.Several
body: Israel has warned Hamas that it will increase strikes on Gaza following concern over launches of kites, drones and balloons from the territory.Several kites were found in an Israeli community near the border with Gaza over the weekend, local media reported."Forceful actions will be taken to put an end to this phenomenon," Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Monday.Before the war, kites and balloons carrying incendiary devices were launched into Israel, causing fires that burned forest and farmland.Hamas has denied responsibility for the new kites - which were not carrying explosives - and said they belonged to "children searching for their innocent childhood amid the rubble".The group also accused Israel of using the kites as a "pretext" for continued air strikes in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreed last October.Four kites were found in Kibbutz Nahal Oz, which is about 800m (2,620ft) from the Gaza border, on Friday and Saturday. Several more were found elsewhere in southern Israel last week, according to local media.The Israeli reports cited military sources as saying they believed Hamas was behind the kites and that they might have been intended to test Israel's response.No suspicious materials were attached to the kites and they did not pose a threat, the military said.But Katz warned there would be "zero tolerance" and said: "A balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone, with or without explosives."Residents of Nahal Oz said in a statement that they feared the return of incendiary kites and balloons, adding: "We will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security."Hamas warned of "the danger of the allegations and threats" from Israel and said the kites were "basically children's toys from displacement camps"."These threats are based on fabricated pretexts and are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people," a spokesman for the group added.On Sunday, Palestinian health officials said two people were killed and seven others injured in two Israeli strikes in Nuseirat refugee camp and the town of al-Zawayda, both in central Gaza.A four-year-old boy called Mohammed Taha was killed when a building in al-Zawayda, just north of Maghazi refugee camp, was bombed, according to local media.The Israeli military said it killed the commander of a Hamas weapons manufacturing site in the Maghazi area, whom it identified as Ismail Abu Ful, and that it had warned the residents to evacuate beforehand."There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," Abu Ahmed, a displaced man who had been sheltering nearby, told Reuters news agency. "We want solutions, we want to live in peace."On Monday, Palestinian media reported that a man called Mohammed Abu Asad was killed in an overnight Israeli strike on a tent in the central town of Deir al-Balah.The Israeli military said Abu Asad was a member of the elite Nukhba forces of Hamas's military wing who had taken part in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the cross-border assault, during which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.More than 74,420 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including 1,288 since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

schema.headline: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza

title: Chan Mathok Atak pleads guilty over Channel boat with 165 migrants
description: A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has pleaded guilty to endangering others duri
body: A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has pleaded guilty to endangering others during a sea crossing.Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally from South Sudan, admitted the offence at Canterbury Crown Court in relation to a crossing on 23 July.Rescuers said they were astonished and alarmed to see the number of people packed onto the dinghy.  It was said to have been about the same length as a bus before it began deflating in the world's busiest shipping lane.Prosecutors said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat. Endangerment at sea is a new offence created to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the Channel.At the time of the crossing, the dinghy set a record for the largest number of people brought over in a single boat since dinghy arrivals began on the south coast in recent years.The figure has since been surpassed, and earlier this month, a record 230 people reached the UK in a so-called "mega dinghy".Atak is due to be sentenced on 11 September.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external,  X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: South Africa v New Zealand: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu drops to bench
description: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has paid the price for an indifferent showing in South Africa's defeat by New Zealand, with the fly-half dropping to the ben
body: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has paid the price for an indifferent showing in South Africa's defeat by New Zealand, with the fly-half dropping to the bench for Saturday's rematch in Cape Town.The All Blacks, revitalised under new coach Dave Rennie, ran out 33-16 winners in the series opener in Johannesburg.Feinberg-Mngomezulu was turned over five times in possession and occasionally exposed in defence, before he shifted to full-back for the Springboks in the second half of Saturday's first Test.South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has recalled 32-year-old double Rugby World Cup winner Handre Pollard at 10, while injuries to Cheslin Kolbe and Grant Williams have brought Ethan Hooker and Cobus Reinach into the starting line-up at wing and scrum-half respectively.Siya Kolisi may return to the back row after recovering from a hamstring injury, but Erasmus has also named Paul de Villiers as a back-up at blindside flanker in case Kolisi is not ready.Thirty-nine year-old Deon Fourie, who came off the bench to play 77 minutes of the Springboks' 2023 Rugby World Cup final win over New Zealand, could win his first cap since that occasion after being named among the replacements."There were a handful of positives and negatives last week, but the main thing that let us down was that we created so many chances, but mistakes at crucial times cost us," said Erasmus."We'll put in a lot of work this week to ensure that we are sharp in that regard this weekend because if we had used even some of those chances, the result could have been completely different."South Africa side to face New Zealand: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Pollard, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi/De Villiers, PS du Toit, Wiese.Replacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, Feinberg-Mngomezulu.New Zealand may be tempted to give Richie Mo'unga an immediate Test return as they chase a 2-0 lead in the four-match series that has been marketed as 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry'.The 32-year-old was first-choice stand-off during their 2023 Rugby World Cup campaign, but he has been ineligible for selection while playing his club rugby in Japan since.However, his signing for Canterbury and the Crusaders, along with an injury to Billy Proctor, has paved the way for his comeback.Mo'unga will start at 10 in Tuesday's match against Johannesburg-based provincial side the Lions.Mo'unga, who says his determination to return to Tests was fuelled by watching a Six Nations match while in a Japanese karaoke bar last year, is confident he can produce the form that earned him a spot in World Rugby's team of 2023."I'm competitive; I want to be the best," he said. "I know that there's a process to that, and at this point in time, the process looks a bit different around preparing someone else [All Blacks' current first-choice fly-half Ruben Love] to be the best."I'm really competitive, but I'm also a team man. Whoever gets the role, gets the role, and if it's not me, I'll do anything I can to help them succeed."This game was always coming for me. There was always going to be a return. I wasn't sure when it was, but mentally I've prepared for my return in the black jersey, and I'm ready."New Zealand side to face Lions: B Barrett; Fineanganofo, Ioane, Tavatavanawai, Narawa; Mo'unga, Hotham; Lauaki, Taukei'aho, Tosi, Darry, Tuipulotu, Sititi, Blackadder, Ta'eiloa.Replacements: Slater, Tu'ungafasi, Ma'u, Hannah, Lakai, Preston, Jacomb, Lienert-Brown.

schema.headline: South Africa v New Zealand: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu drops to bench

title: Brydon Carse dropped from England squad for second Test v Pakistan after nightclub incident
description: Pace bowler Brydon Carse has been removed from England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan amid an ongoing investigation into an incident tha
body: Pace bowler Brydon Carse has been removed from England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan amid an ongoing investigation into an incident that led to him being handcuffed by police.Images that appeared on social media on Sunday showed Carse, 31, in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby on Saturday night.The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has referred the incident to the Cricket Regulator.The Regulator will investigate and, as a result, Carse has been removed from the squad and replaced by Sonny Baker.It is the latest in a string of off-field incidents involving the England team - Carse has become the third player this summer to miss a Test because of a disciplinary issue."Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby," said an ECB statement."Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."Carse was part of the England squad for the first Test against Pakistan, which the hosts won by an innings inside three days at Headingley.When he was not named in the starting XI, Carse was released to play for Durham away at Derbyshire, a game the Division Two leaders won on Saturday evening.Following that win, Carse was filmed in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby. It has not been confirmed why he was detained, though he was released without charge.The incident occurred less than 48 hours before Carse was scheduled to arrive in London to join up with the rest of the England squad for the second Test at Lord's.Also in the footage was Carse's Durham team-mate Matthew Potts, while former England captain Ben Stokes could be seen in the background. Though Stokes has retired from international cricket, he is still under a central contract with the ECB, as are Potts and Carse.In June, Stokes and Gus Atkinson were present in a London nightclub when a member of England's security staff was struck by a Saracens rugby player.Both men missed the second Test against New Zealand while the incident was investigated, and the pair were eventually given a written warning as to their conduct.Stokes and Atkinson breached an England team curfew that was introduced following late-night incidents during the winter.Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington and Ben Duckett was filmed, apparently drunk, on England's Ashes holiday in Noosa.On replacing Stokes as England captain, Joe Root began his second spell in charge by removing the curfew. Guidelines issued to players on the consumption of alcohol around matches and in public were also relaxed.On the day before the first Test against Pakistan, Root called on his players to be "really good role models and good human beings"."You always want to represent your country in the best possible light," Root told BBC Sport."We might have fallen short of that on a few occasions in the recent past. The only thing we can do to rectify that is be really good role models, good human beings and put in really strong performances on the field."In the summer of 2024, Carse was given a three-month ban for historical betting offences.He has subsequently rebuilt his career to become an England regular across formats. Since Carse made his Test debut in October 2024, no England bowler has taken more than his 58 wickets.It is unlikely Carse would have played at Lord's - instead he would probably have been a back-up to England's four frontline seamers from Headingley.His omission means another opportunity for 23-year-old Baker, who won his only Test cap in the second match of the series against New Zealand in June.

schema.headline: Brydon Carse dropped from England squad for second Test v Pakistan after nightclub incident

title: 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war
description: Cindy Baldassi relies on American buyers to keep her stone-and-glass jewellery company going. Some 75% of sales of pieces including amethyst, sea glas
body: Cindy Baldassi relies on American buyers to keep her stone-and-glass jewellery company going. Some 75% of sales of pieces including amethyst, sea glass and agates from her business, CindyLouWho2, based in Calgary, Alberta, come from Americans. But after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed over the weekend and leaders of both countries pledged to slap 50% tariffs on each other's products, business owners on both sides of the border are bracing for the fallout.With a majority of the items she sells falling under US President Donald Trump's newly imposed tariffs, Baldassi says she will need to add 50% to the price of most of her products to stay afloat. "It's quite likely that it will wipe out most of my US sales," Baldassi told the BBC. "I expect that at least half of my business will be gone." Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged levies starting on 8 September on US steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. Trump tariffs went into effect on Saturday, hitting Canadian wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.Like many retailers, Matteo Sgaramella, founder of Toronto-based menswear brand Outclass, told the BBC that his company collects orders from clothing designers months before they are due to arrive in stores. Products that US stores ordered in January will arrive in September but now with a new tariff. "If I contact them now and tell them, hey, you know, you may get an extra 50% bill from UPS on top of what you need to pay me for this shipment, they're all going to say, 'no way, don't ship it,'" Sgaramella said.He still has to figure out where that additional cost will go. "There's going to be a lot of people that go out of business because of this," Sgaramella said, but noted that only 20% of his wholesale sales and 20% of his e-commerce come from the US."Big business can, you know, always find a way... but small businesses are going to get smashed by this."Those pillows are their best-selling gift item, retailing at $59. With the newly imposed tariffs, a normal markup would bring the price of that pillow to somewhere between $86 and $90, Osgood told the BBC. "Gift items are really price-point sensitive; people have in their mind what they're going to pay for a gift, and they're not going to pay more than that," Roach said. The couple, whose shop has been operating for 51 years, say they will likely hold the original price and hope the "tariff problem," as Roach calls it, gets worked out. "It would be one thing if we had three months' notice; that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors, but when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck," he said. While the tariffs could mean changes for the Paloma Clothing company, other American companies are facing the same battle they have faced since Trump returned to office and began imposing his levies. Bill Easton, owner of Terre Rouge Wines in Plymouth, California, has been unable to ship his wine north to Canada for the past year and a half due to a boycott of US alcohol. He is currently paying $2,400 a month to store that wine in a warehouse in the hope that he will one day be able to ship it to the Canadian markets he sells to. "The wine has just gotten better in the warehouse, but I can't expect my customer in Canada to pay that extra cost that I've assumed over the last year and a half as part of the price, if I was able to sell it tomorrow," Easton told the BBC.And then there are the American businesses impacted by proximity to the Canadian border. The number of Canadian customers travelling across the border to shop at Heather Seevers' craft shop, Northwest Yarns and Mercantile in Bellingham, Washington, has gone down some 20% since the tariff war began over a year ago. What has further irked Canadians has been Trump musing on Canada becoming a 51st US state. The shop sits 25 minutes from the US-Canada border and since the "war" ensued Seevers said her business received emails from Canadian customers saying they could not patronise her business "due to anti-Canadian rhetoric"."We completely understood that," she said. But the combined impact of fewer customers and higher prices has left the shop asking for help from the community recently via a fundraising initiative to stay afloat. And then, over the weekend, when the new tariffs struck, Seevers saw another hurdle appear."It's going to get worse before it gets better," she said. "It's going to take years and years and years to get a relationship back with Canada, and I think these new tariffs are digging us deeper into a hole."Additional reporting from Nadine Yousif

schema.headline: 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

title: All Points East: EsDeeKid mystery no problem for rapper's fans
description: EsDeeKid dropped his debut album Rebel in June 2025 but it took a few months to cut through into the mainstream - first appearing at number 82 in the
body: EsDeeKid dropped his debut album Rebel in June 2025 but it took a few months to cut through into the mainstream - first appearing at number 82 in the UK Official Albums Charts.It's since gone on to reach number eight, while also peaking at 23 on the Billboard 200 chart in the US.By the end of last year, EsDeeKid's monthly listens on Spotify had "skyrocketed", external, which Dazed said had "half of Europe rapping in his distinctive scouse accent".Danil Boparai, a content strategy director at Dazed, thinks "the hype is justified"."He brings a very raw energy which you see with his reluctance to do much press, no-one knows much about him, it's all about the music for him," he says."EsDeeKid has become one of the voices of Gen Z musically, through a unique take on rap due to his Scouse accent and his aesthetic taps into quite medieval-style fashion."He had a castle style set [on Sunday] which was quite unique, I haven't see that at All Points East or Outbreak festival before." It helps that every song on the musician's debut mixtape "became like a TikTok anthem", Boparai says.And his appeal has since spread across the pond. EsDeeKid's tour will begin in North America in September, before ending in December with two hometown shows in Liverpool.For fan James, the anonymity element is "amazing"."I work in event promotion, I think giving yourself an aesthetic, something to cling to, something that people can watch is really important in the music industry, it makes you stand out," he says.Decked out in a bright outfit to see EsDeeKid, fan Zari says the rapper's presence is "very mysterious". "But that's the good thing about him, it's what brings people towards him, we're all curious." And for Boparai, the Chalamet rumours may have been big for his brand, but having the music to back it up is crucial. "EsDeeKid understands the internet," he says. "It is so important to come across as truly authentic and I think he does because he lets his music do the speaking for him."He also doesn't change his accent, he doesn't reveal his face."He's just him, take it or leave it."

schema.headline: All Points East: EsDeeKid mystery no problem for rapper's fans

title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
description: The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI a
body: The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July. Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall."We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our £2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

schema.headline: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests

title: Harvey Elliott: Does Liverpool midfielder have an Anfield future after Newcastle omission?
description: It was a little under a month ago when in the bowels of the Yankee Stadium in New York, Harvey Elliott spoke candidly about his emotions after a "toug
body: It was a little under a month ago when in the bowels of the Yankee Stadium in New York, Harvey Elliott spoke candidly about his emotions after a "tough" loan spell at Aston Villa and why this summer felt like a second chance for Liverpool.There was a smile on his face when he spoke about his love for the club - the team he has supported since he was a boy - and wanting to be free and enjoying himself again with his football, because he felt like he had not done that enough.You only had to see Elliott's joy when he came off the bench in Liverpool's friendly against Monaco earlier this month as all four sides of Anfield stood up and applauded to see what it meant.With a number of senior first-team players absent, Elliott started Liverpool's first friendly under Andoni Iraola in Nashville and again when Liverpool took on Wrexham in New York four days later but as the World Cup contingent returned, the midfielder was benched and where he stood in the squad became clearer.On the first weekend of the Premier League season, Elliott was left out of the Liverpool squad entirely for their trip to Newcastle and it now looks increasingly likely that the 23-year-old could be on his way out before the transfer window ends.Liverpool have received no offers for Elliott - who spent last season on loan at Aston Villa - and his exclusion from the squad on Sunday was not transfer related, nor is the midfielder carrying an injury. Elliott's contract expires next summer and if first-team football is not possible at Liverpool he needs to go somewhere where it is, to avoid another lost season.In America, Elliott spoke about how we would speak to Iraola at the "right time" and emphasised the need to be "selfish". "Ultimately, I'm still wanting to be selfish, doing what's right for me," said Elliott. "Whether that's staying here and fighting for my place or potentially going elsewhere, I'm still unsure at the moment until I get some more intel."Another year on the fringes would be no good for the man who was named player of the tournament when England Under-21s won the European Championship in 2025.By now, much has been said about his situation at Villa last season which Unai Emery described as "embarrassing" for all involved. Elliott played only nine games and a total of 277 minutes after Villa decided early on in the campaign that they did not want to trigger an obligation to sign him from Liverpool for £35m if he made 10 appearances.Those at Villa stressed Elliott's professionalism and his positivity throughout and to his credit, the attacking midfielder returned early to Liverpool for the start of pre-season after a personally-challenging year. Iraola himself was impressed by his attitude, saying as much in his introductory press conference."I've seen him with this eagerness to show himself. He will have a chance during the pre-season. He came one week earlier and I hope we can see him in a good place," said Iraola. "Last season had to have been very difficult for him as it was a strange situation that meant they [Aston Villa] couldn't let him play."In effect, the move to Villa wasted a season of Elliott's career even if he was adamant that it was a "learning curve" in a year where Villa won the Europa League."I don't wish it upon any other player, because it's not nice at all," Elliott said. When he left Liverpool last summer, the primary factor was more game-time after making just one Premier League start during Liverpool's title-winning campaign under Arne Slot in 2024-25. So with a week to go of the transfer window and with further attacking signings expected at Anfield, perhaps the writing is on the wall. A move lower down the Premier League or somewhere in Europe may be an option. After all, this is a player who scored the winner for Liverpool at PSG in a year where the Ligue 1 club won the Champions League. He is neat on the ball and unafraid to take risks - a return of 15 goals and 21 assists for Liverpool, across all competitions, showcases what he can do.Either way, it is imperative for all involved that Elliott finds somewhere to play football regularly this season because it seems unlikely at Liverpool and at 23, he cannot afford to have a season like last.

schema.headline: Harvey Elliott: Does Liverpool midfielder have an Anfield future after Newcastle omission?

title: Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints as he visits Kyiv
description: Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from RussiaImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham accepts an award fro
body: Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from RussiaImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham accepts an award from Volodymyr Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for UkraineByHenry Moore and Imogen JamesUpdated 31 minutes agoAndy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime minister.Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.He said the coalition was "doing everything we can" while urging the US Congress to "ratchet up" economic pressure on Russia.The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.During the meeting with France and Ukraine, Burnham said allies were doing "everything we can" to "dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks" of air defences to protect Ukraine."This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, praising the "strength" of the Ukrainian people. "Ukraine has been Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe."It comes after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them."Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it."He added the issue of missile interceptors would be the main topic at the coalition of the willing meeting. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Burnham chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing" in KyivBurnham has been reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people. In a joint statement after the meeting, Burham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgenty priority".They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".It came as the European Union said it had released €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defences. The finance is part of a wider €90bn loan from the EU to Ukraine.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham lays flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a Monday serviceOn Monday morning the prime minister laid flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a service at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.He accepted an award from Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine during an independence day event outside the St Sofia cathedral in Kyiv. In a speech, Burnham compared Ukraine's resistance to Russia to the UK's fight with Nazi Germany, saying: "My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st."In a statement issued ahead of the visit, the prime minister said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes."I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."Moscow earlier warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure.Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesThe government is allowing UK defence company MBDA to declassify information on its components for the Scalp missile.The long-range missile weighs 1,300kg and is 16.7ft (5.10m) in length. It is capable of hitting targets around 150 miles into Russia - not as far as Ukraine's deep strike drone capability but it is a significant step in showing the willingness of international partners to share weapons technology.The maker describes them as designed to hit pre-planned, stationary targets. It can be used day and night in all weather, and has advanced navigation systems. MBDA adds that it is in service with the Royal Air Force, the French Air Force, Italian Air Force and has been used in Iraq, Syria and Libya. What are the Storm Shadow missiles Ukraine has fired into Russia?Ukraine hopes it can also be given more Patriot interceptor missiles, with Zelensky again asking for more of the weapon, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles. On Sunday, he said they have requested 360 of the missiles, but are "working with countries on additional options". Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriots, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.While the Scalp missile does not intercept enemy attacks like the Patriots, Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast they were sharing its blueprints so Ukraine could "defend against this illegal invasion that's now killed so many people"."It's not just the front lines, it's shopping centres, it's housing that's being targeted by Russia in their illegal war and that's why we have said and we will continue to make sure our actions follow it that we will support Ukraine for as long as it takes," he added.Pollard said Ukraine is in need of a variety of weapons, which is why the UK is supplying other air defence assets to take down Russian cruise missiles, and counter-drone measures.Figure caption, Watch: Burnham pledges support in first meeting with ZelenskyThe Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay".In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change."Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me".The visit comes as Russia confirmed its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in London in recent weeks.The Kremlin is yet to put forward a replacement but Russia's embassy to the UK told the BBC it did not reflect an intention to downgrade diplomatic relations between the two nations.Deadly exchanges between Russia and Ukraine continued overnight, with two children killed and seven injured when Ukrainian drone debris hit a private children's centre in Russia, local authorities say.A warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon was also set on fire, two days after Ukraine said it would target the company for selling dual use items that could be used by the military.It was at the third night in the row that Ozon's warehouses had been targeted, with the company confirming on Saturday that a logistics centre in the Samara region had been hit and a warehouse in Orenburg on Sunday.Three people were also killed in a Russian attack on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
description: Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to de
body: Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it prohibits posts encouraging participation in high-risk challenges, including driving against traffic, and takes down such content once made aware.It said it also restrict users under 18 from seeing content not suitable to them, such as posts depicting any sort of reckless driving.The BBC has also contacted X for comment.On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that"."It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves."Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

title: Fulham v Chelsea:  Rafa Benitez on former players Alonso and Arbeloa as managers
description: When former Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez is asked whether he had expected his then-players Xabi Alonso and Alvaro Arbeloa to become managers, his
body: When former Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez is asked whether he had expected his then-players Xabi Alonso and Alvaro Arbeloa to become managers, his response is brutally honest."Alonso, yes. Arbeloa, not really," he says. "For me, Arbeloa was a surprise."Almost 20 years after Benitez brought them together at Anfield, the pair will go head-to-head as Arbeloa's Fulham host Alonso's Chelsea on Monday.The pair won the 2010 World Cup and two European Championships with Spain, along with domestic league and cup triumphs when they both joined Real Madrid after Liverpool.They played together for seven years at club level and shared the pitch 262 times for club and country, and their careers have remained closely intertwined since.Arbeloa was promoted from Real Madrid B to replace Alonso when he was sacked by the Spanish giants in January last season."He was in Castilla [Real Madrid's academy], which was similar to how I started, and then he went to Madrid in special circumstances," Benitez said of Arbeloa's rise to Real manager.They both returned to England in July to take up their first Premier League managerial roles and now lead clubs whose stadiums are only two miles apart."With Alvaro, he knows the Premier League," Benitez told BBC Sport. "But his experience is shorter than Xabi's. We need to know how he can cope outside Real Madrid, which protects you in a way. Outside, you are on your own."It's no surprise that, having played as team-mates – including under Jose Mourinho and Carlo Ancelotti at Real Madrid, and Vicente del Bosque with Spain – socialised off the pitch and even gone on holiday together, the pair are, in the words of Arbeloa, "very good friends", despite being "rivals when the game starts". He explained they spoke to each other in the lead up to Monday's match, but not about football. Other similarities will see the duo live close to each other in Cobham, Surrey, with their children attending the same school.In the words of Arbeloa, their friendship "will never change".Alonso was one of Benitez's first Liverpool signings in 2004 as he looked to overhaul Gerard Houllier's squad, Arbeloa then joining in 2007 from Deportivo after rising through the ranks at Real Madrid.Benitez explained that Alonso has experience of "coaching at a different level in a different country", having had success in the Bundesliga at Bayer Leverkusen by winning a league and cup double in 2024.Alonso, in particular, had "vision" on the pitch, says Benitez, while his experiences playing at Liverpool, Real Madrid and then under Pep Guardiola at Bayern Munich would have "opened his mind" to a range of coaching approaches.Benitez recalls a moment of magic from Alonso in a 2009 game that displayed his football intelligence.In a match against Sam Allardyce's Blackburn at Anfield, Alonso ignored an instruction to deliver a free-kick to the far post. Instead, his ball to the near post allowed Fernando Torres to head in his second goal of the match as Liverpool went on to win 4-0."He was someone who was always thinking," said Benitez.It is not just Alonso and Arbeloa who are among Benitez's former Liverpool players to have moved into management.He reels off more than 20 names who have become coaches or managers, a list including Wales boss Craig Bellamy. He also points out that Djimi Traore is now an assistant coach at Seattle Sounders."I sent him to the shower at half-time in the Champions League final [in 2005]," he recalled of the defender, who was expecting to be substituted after a poor first-half before an injury to Steve Finnan saw him reinstated for Liverpool's historic second-half comeback and eventual victory on penalties against AC Milan in 2005.He added: "They always take something from you. Maybe two or three things they can use [as a coach], and I'm happy with that."It has been more than 40 years since Benitez began coaching at Real Madrid and, this summer, he finds himself in the unusual position of being without a job.Now 66, Benitez says he is "waiting for another challenge", adding that his passion for the game is undiminished, as is his desire to "improve teams and players".He felt he delivered in his most recent role at Panathinaikos, securing the top-four finish he had been tasked with achieving when he took the job in October, but was still sacked in May.Explaining his continued motivation, Benitez said: "I was a PE teacher before and was trying to improve young people. It was the same as when I had Anthony Gordon at Everton."The former Newcastle and Chelsea manager remains a Uefa technical observer and speaks about adapting to the modern game, using social media, artificial intelligence and increasingly sophisticated data as part of his approach."I had some offers," Benitez said, having recently been linked with the Scotland job."Maybe it is a national team, as a lot of teams will change after the World Cup, but there has to be something where you feel you can achieve something, whether that is promotion, like we had at Newcastle, with amazing fans."I know football now is more demanding. You have to be patient because, if not, if you change with the pressure of social media and change every seven months, then you don't have any project. That is the difficult thing."

title: Julian Alvarez transfer news: Arsenal, Barcelona or Atletico Madrid stay for striker?
description: Acrimony, anger and animosity; the Julian Alvarez summer transfer saga in a nutshell.The boos aimed at the Atletico Madrid forward from his own suppor
body: Acrimony, anger and animosity; the Julian Alvarez summer transfer saga in a nutshell.The boos aimed at the Atletico Madrid forward from his own supporters at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday provided the latest twist in what has been one of the most bitter - and certainly public - storylines of the window.And with deadline day on 1 September, the Argentine World Cup winner's future remains one of the hottest topics.In simplistic terms the dispute comes down to this; Alvarez wants to join Barcelona - but Atletico won't let him.The Madrid club's steadfast refusal to sanction the 26-year-old's dream move to the Spotify Camp Nou has led to one of the most rancorous public falling-outs in recent memory.The feud led to Atleti fans jeering their own player on his return to club action after the summer World Cup in a 2-2 home draw with Villarreal on Sunday.It had been anticipated.Atletico Madrid president Enrique Cerezo, speaking last week, said: "I don't know if he will say sorry, but Julian is an excellent person and I am absolutely sure that he will win over the fans in two games."I said he wouldn't be sold, he's our player and an important part of our team. We like that he's with us and think he will have a magnificent season."Nevertheless, the events that unfolded on Sunday certainly haven't gone unnoticed at Arsenal.BBC Sport has consistently reported over the summer that Alvarez is viewed as the Gunners' dream transfer target.But for the vast majority of the window, Arsenal's interest has been largely dormant because they were fully aware of his desire to join Barcelona.They have been waiting for the right moment to strike and those at the Emirates are hopeful that time may be coming.But is the deal possible?Arsenal are realistic about their chances of signing Alvarez before next week's transfer deadline.Do they want him? Yes. Are they trying? Yes. Can they pull it off? The answer to that question is less unequivocal.Manager Mikel Arteta and sporting director Andrea Berta know it is a long shot, not least because former Manchester City forward Alvarez, at least so far, has shown little indication he would be willing to join the club.His current reluctance to give the green light on a move to London isn't necessarily linked to any apprehension towards Arsenal - but rather that doing so would see him forgoing his dream of joining Barcelona.Alvarez has also been made aware of certain visa regulations that would create difficulty for his family visiting him in the UK.Moving to Catalonia is what he truly wants. What's more, the Camp Nou club are absolutely willing to make that happen.But Atleti are absolutely adamant they will not sell Alvarez to Barcelona.In May, they made a series of social media posts brutally mocking the pursuit by the Spanish champions of their player to millions of followers."Don't believe everything you see, especially if it's related to Barca," Atletico posted. "In recent months, we've been suffering a smear campaign against one of our players."For the Madrid side, the matter is closed and that leaves Alvarez's dream in serious jeopardy.Therein lies a slither of hope for Arsenal because, as things stand, the only way out is a move to the Emirates Stadium.Indeed, according to well-placed sources there has been a slight softening of Alvarez's stance in recent days, although not enough yet to get anyone at Arsenal excited.But should he change his mind in the final days of the window, then the Gunners are poised.Since the start of the summer, according to BBC Sport sources, Arsenal have been confident Alvarez's move to Barcelona was a non-starter.But while he still harboured hope of fulfilling that ambition, Arteta's men focused on the captures of Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa, while also trying to bring Real Madrid attacker Vinicius Jr to London.With the Brazilian extending his contract to stay in Spain, Arsenal have now decided to step things up regarding Alvarez.Atleti director Mateu Alemany was in London last week, where he is understood to have met with Arsenal counterparts - and made clear his side would seek a fee of 150m euros (£128m). The Gunners are confident they can finance any deal and quickly finalise the transfer - if he said yes.Arteta is fully aware if Alvarez was to join Arsenal this summer he would only be doing so because his preferred destination was not possible.It is understood the Spaniard is comfortable with that scenario and believes Alvarez would eventually become fully invested and committed to the Arsenal project.The ball is now in Alvarez's court. If he wants to leave Atletico, which sources close to the attacker insist that he does, then the Premier League champions appear to be his only option.Alvarez joined Atletico for £81m from Manchester City in August 2024, having spent just over two years at the Etihad following a £14.1 move from Argentine side River Plate.He won six major trophies at City - including the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023 - scoring 36 goals in 106 appearances.At Atletico, he has scored 49 goals in 107 appearances, but has not yet won any silverware.Could Alvarez also concede defeat in his efforts to leave Atleti this summer and attempt to mend what appears to be a broken relationship with the club and its supporters?It is possible, although, according to those close to the player, it is his belief that the Madrid club are being unreasonable. Indeed the player's agent Fernando Hidalgo has been open with his disdain towards how his client has been treated this summer.That said, Alvarez is described as a private individual and said to be deeply uncomfortable about the very public nature of the conflict with his club - although the player himself also outlined his desire to leave publicly during the World Cup."A transfer is the best option," he said.When Real Madrid released a statement on 9 June saying they had an offer of 150m euros (£128m) rejected by their neighbours, there was a sense from the Alvarez camp Atletico had reneged on an agreement to let the striker leave if they received an offer of that amount.Of course, the prospect of selling Alvarez to their fiercest rivals was viewed as a non-starter by Atletico.For South Americans - playing for Real or Barca represents the holy grail.Hansi Flick's side remain interested in Alvarez, but fear Atletico's stance isn't purely posturing and have started to consider alternative options, including Arsenal's Swedish striker Viktor Gyokeres.If they decide to turn their attention elsewhere, Alvarez will have a decision to make.Arsenal or nothing? We'll have the answer soon.

title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
description: Figure caption, Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"ByKawoon Khamoos
body: Figure caption, Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"ByKawoon KhamooshBBC World ServiceReporting fromSheberghan, Kabul and KandaharGovernor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.She will not take no for an answer.In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses."If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says.After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.Image caption, The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several years In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage."Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour.""Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.Image source, EPA/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, A hole left by the destruction of one of the Buddha statues in Bamiyan -  Sarhadi says he destroyed itSarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands."Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul."I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.Image caption, Habibullah Badr says that in the past he was involved in operations involving suicide attacksHe is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn."Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."The Taliban: Coming Out of the ShadowsAudiences in the UK can watch on iPlayer from 17:00 and on Global Eye on BBC Two at 19:00Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.Image caption, Zabihullah Mujahid says women's rights and freedom of speech need to be seen "through the Sharia lens"He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it".When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.Image caption, Abid Lalai is one of many Taliban fighters who hid out in caves to evade capture under previous governmentsHis superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics."Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem."I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power."Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever.""I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

schema.headline: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
